opus-5.5.text:
I think the most useful way to approach it is to stop thinking about jobs as single units and instead think about them as bundles of tasks. A job is really a collection of many different things a person does over the course of a week, and AI systems tend to get good at tasks unevenly. So the question becomes: what fraction of the tasks in a given job can be done well by AI, and how hard is the remaining residue?

A few factors seem to matter a lot. One is whether the work can be done entirely on a computer. Remote, digital work is much more exposed in the near term than anything that requires physical manipulation in messy, unstructured environments. Robotics has lagged behind progress in language and reasoning, and I'd expect that gap to persist for a while, so jobs like plumbing, construction, or elder care are probably going to be automated later than a lot of office work, even though people's intuitions used to point the other way.

Another factor is how long the time horizon of the tasks is and how much context they require. Current systems are quite good at short, well-specified tasks, but they struggle more with things that require keeping coherent plans over days or weeks, accumulating context about an organization, adapting when things go wrong, and exercising judgment without clear feedback. So jobs that consist mostly of short, self-contained tasks with clear success criteria will go first, and jobs requiring long-horizon agency will take longer.

Related to that is the availability of training data and feedback signals. Where you have lots of examples or where you can easily check whether an output is correct, as in coding or math, progress tends to be fast. Where the quality of work is hard to evaluate, or where the relevant knowledge is tacit and never written down, it's slower.

Then there are non-technical factors that I think people sometimes underweight, like regulation, liability, and preferences for a human in the loop. Even if an AI can technically do much of what a doctor or a lawyer does, licensing requirements and legal accountability can delay actual deployment. And there are some roles where people may simply value a human doing the job, though I'd be cautious about assuming that protects very many jobs in the long run, because economic pressure tends to be strong.

Finally, I'd emphasize that partial automation doesn't necessarily mean job loss right away. If AI handles part of a job, the human might become more productive and focus on the remaining bottleneck tasks. The real displacement tends to come when the last critical pieces get automated. So the question of which jobs go first is really about which jobs have the fewest of those hard bottleneck tasks remaining.

r001.rationale: It says work requiring physical manipulation in messy environments, such as plumbing or construction, is likely to be automated later.

r002.rationale: It says tasks requiring coherent plans over days or weeks and long-horizon agency take longer to automate.

r003.rationale: It discusses uneven AI capability across tasks, but does not identify large differences in human performance at a job as a reason for earlier automation.

r004.rationale: It describes jobs as bundles of tasks that AI handles unevenly, with remaining bottleneck tasks delaying full automation.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most useful frame is to stop thinking about jobs as units and start thinking about tasks, and then ask what makes a task hard for current systems. When you do that, a few dimensions fall out.

The first is how much of the task can be done with the kind of data we actually have. Language models got good at writing and coding because there's an enormous corpus of text and code on the internet, and the task structure maps very directly onto what's in the training data. If a job consists mostly of taking in text, reasoning about it, and producing text, that's going to go early. If a job requires acting in the physical world, the data situation is much worse. We don't have the equivalent of the internet for manipulating objects, and collecting that data is slow and expensive. So I expect physical work to lag, not because it's intellectually harder in some deep sense, but because the data bottleneck is real.

The second dimension is how long the horizon is and how expensive mistakes are. Models today are quite good at tasks that take a human a few minutes or maybe an hour, and they degrade as the task stretches to days or weeks, where you need to maintain context, notice you've gone wrong, and recover. A lot of jobs look like short tasks on paper but are really long chains of those tasks with a lot of implicit coordination holding them together. Those will take longer to automate than the surface description suggests.

The third thing I'd point to is how easy it is to verify the output. Where you can check the result cheaply, whether code runs, whether a proof is valid, whether a prediction came true, you can train against that signal and you can also deploy with less human oversight. Where quality is fuzzy or only shows up much later, like management or a lot of advisory work, adoption is slower because the person paying for it can't tell whether they got something good.

And then there's a whole layer that isn't about capability at all. Regulation, liability, who's accountable when something goes wrong, how much the existing workflow has to be rebuilt to actually use the tool. Even if the model can technically do the thing, if the firm has to reorganize its whole process to capture the value, that diffuses over years, not months. Historically that's been true of every major technology, and I don't see a strong reason to think AI is completely exempt from it, although it might compress the timeline.

So if you put that together, my rough ordering is: things that are text-heavy, short-horizon, easily verified, and low-stakes go first. Things that are physical, long-horizon, hard to verify, and high-stakes go last. Most real jobs are a mix, and the interesting question is usually which parts of a job get peeled off, rather than whether the job disappears wholesale.

r001.rationale: It says physical work is expected to lag because data for manipulating objects is scarce and expensive to collect.

r002.rationale: It identifies long task horizons and chains of tasks requiring context, coordination, and recovery as harder to automate.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss large differences in human performance at a job as a reason for earlier automation.

r004.rationale: It says most jobs combine tasks with different automation prospects, so parts of a job may be automated before others.

astra-6.text:
I think the useful starting point is to look at tasks rather than job titles. A job is usually a bundle of different things, and AI might become very good at some of those things while still being unable to do the whole job reliably.

One distinction is how easy it is to check whether the work is correct. If you can give an AI a task, evaluate the result cheaply, and have it try again when it fails, that’s a favorable setting for automation. Parts of programming have that property, for example, though passing tests isn’t the same as knowing that a whole software system does what you want.

Another distinction is how much context the task requires. Something that can be specified clearly and completed on a computer is generally easier to automate than something that requires understanding an organization’s unwritten practices, negotiating with people, or dealing with an unfamiliar physical environment.

But technical capability is only part of the story. You also have to ask whether automation is cheaper, how costly mistakes are, and how much the workflow has to change to accommodate it. So I wouldn’t expect a clean sequence where one entire profession disappears and then another does. I’d expect particular tasks to become cheaper, jobs to change around that, and full automation to happen where the remaining tasks don’t create a substantial bottleneck.

r001.rationale: The response says tasks requiring an unfamiliar physical environment are harder to automate than clearly specified computer tasks.

r002.rationale: It does not mention complex or long-horizon planning as a factor in automation timing.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss differences in human performance at a job.

r004.rationale: It says jobs bundle different tasks that AI may handle unevenly, but does not identify complementary skills as the reason those differences matter.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful starting point is to look at tasks rather than whole jobs. A job usually consists of a bundle of things, and AI might become very good at some of those while still being unable to do the others. So being able to automate a large fraction of someone’s work doesn’t necessarily mean you can replace that person.

One distinction I would look at is how easy it is to check whether the work has been done correctly. If you can give the system a task, evaluate its output cheaply, and have it try again when it fails, that’s a much easier setting for automation. If evaluating the output requires almost as much expertise and effort as doing the task yourself, then the economic benefit is less clear.

Another is how long the system has to operate independently. Doing something useful for five minutes is different from reliably carrying out a project over several weeks, dealing with unexpected problems along the way. Jobs that require that kind of sustained autonomy could take longer to automate, even if the individual steps don’t look especially difficult.

And then there’s the distinction between capability and adoption. Even once a system can do the work, you still need to integrate it into an organization, establish that it’s reliable enough, and work out who is responsible when something goes wrong. So I’d be cautious about producing a simple ranking of occupations. I’d look at the tasks involved, the reliability required, and the practical cost of deploying a system to do them.

r001.rationale: The response does not identify physical work as a reason a job may be automated later.

r002.rationale: It says jobs requiring sustained autonomy over several weeks may take longer to automate, but does not identify complex, long-horizon planning as the reason.

r003.rationale: The response does not discuss variation in human performance as a factor that could make automation earlier.

r004.rationale: It explains that jobs bundle tasks and AI may perform some while remaining unable to perform others, clearly identifying complementary skills with different automation difficulty.
